items.prompt: Meridian and Halcyon's design docs looked equally fine on day one. What actually explains the difference that showed up four months later?
choices: Halcyon's engineers were individually less careful people than Meridian's
Meridian spent 30 minutes threat-modeling before the design doc was written, closing gaps Halcyon's design left open until a pentest found them
Halcyon's feature was simply more complex to build
There was no real difference — the four-month gap was coincidence
items.explanation: The two teams weren't different in skill or effort on the feature itself — the difference was a specific, repeatable habit: Meridian's process required naming threats and mitigations before the design was finalized. Nothing about the code Halcyon wrote was 'careless' in the moment; the gap existed because nothing in their process asked the question before it shipped.
items.reference:
Meridian

30-min threat model before the doc — allowlist, random keys, private bucket baked in

Halcyon

No security section — identical on day one, gap found by a pentest 4 months later

Why: the same gap costs far less to close before code exists than after.

items.prompt: Why does this unit call threat modeling a 'design-time' activity specifically, rather than just 'a security practice'?
choices: Because it can only be legally performed by a dedicated security team
Because its whole value comes from happening before code exists, when a threat can still change the design itself instead of requiring a retrofit or a patch
Because 'design-time' just means it takes a long time to do
There's no meaningful distinction — any security activity counts as design-time
items.explanation: The timing is the entire point. A threat found before implementation changes what gets built (a deny-by-default allowlist instead of a blocklist added later); the identical threat found after implementation requires a patch, a re-review, and often a rollout — much more expensive for the same underlying fix.
items.reference:
Meridian

30-min threat model before the doc — allowlist, random keys, private bucket baked in

Halcyon

No security section — identical on day one, gap found by a pentest 4 months later

Why: the same gap costs far less to close before code exists than after.

items.prompt: A team argues they don't need design-time threat modeling because `security-testing` already runs SAST/DAST scans before every release. What's the gap in that argument?
choices: There's no gap — automated scanning fully replaces design-time threat modeling

Scanning finds bugs in code that already exists; it can't tell a team that a design itself is missing a mitigation, like a permissive-by-default field, until code implementing that design has already been written
Scanning is strictly more thorough than any threat model could ever be
Scanning and threat modeling test the exact same things, just at different speeds
items.explanation: SAST/DAST verify code that already exists against known bug patterns — they're powerful, but structurally downstream of the design decision itself. A design that's permissive by default, or that never scopes a service account tightly, isn't a 'bug' a scanner pattern-matches against; it's a decision that has to be caught earlier, at the point where the decision is still being made.
items.reference:
Meridian

30-min threat model before the doc — allowlist, random keys, private bucket baked in

Halcyon

No security section — identical on day one, gap found by a pentest 4 months later

Why: the same gap costs far less to close before code exists than after.

items.prompt: What does the 'S' in STRIDE stand for, and what question does it ask about a design?
choices: Scalability — can the system handle enough load?
Spoofing — can someone pretend to be a legitimate user or service?
Storage — is data stored efficiently?
Sanitization — is user input cleaned before use?
items.explanation: Spoofing is specifically about impersonation — can an attacker present themselves as someone (or something) they're not, whether that's another user, a legitimate service, or the system itself. It's the first of STRIDE's six threat categories, not a general catch-all for input handling.
items.reference:
SpoofingTamperingRepudiationInfo disclosureDenial of serviceElevation of privilege

Why: each letter is a distinct question, asked at every element of a design.

items.prompt: What does STRIDE's 'E' (Elevation of privilege) ask about a design?
choices: Whether the system's error messages are helpful to developers
Whether an action can end up with more access or capability than it should have had
Whether the system can be exported to a different cloud provider
Whether encryption is used at rest
items.explanation: Elevation of privilege asks whether something — a user, a process, an uploaded file — can end up acting with more authority than it was granted, such as an uploaded file executing with the same privileges as the service that stored it. It's distinct from Spoofing (pretending to be someone else) even though both involve gaining access that shouldn't be available.
items.reference:
SpoofingTamperingRepudiationInfo disclosureDenial of serviceElevation of privilege

Why: each letter is a distinct question, asked at every element of a design.

items.prompt: What is a 'trust boundary' in a data-flow diagram?
choices: The line separating frontend code from backend code
Any point where data crosses from one level of trust to another — for example, a public request reaching an internal API
The boundary of a company's legal jurisdiction
A firewall rule written in a specific configuration file
items.explanation: A trust boundary marks a change in trust level, not necessarily a change in technology or team ownership — an anonymous browser handing bytes to an authenticated API is a trust boundary crossing regardless of what's on either side technically.
items.reference:
Untrusted: student's browser
App trust: upload API, scan queue
Storage trust: private bucket

Why: threats cluster where trust level changes, not inside a single trusted zone.

items.prompt: Why do threats cluster at trust boundaries rather than spreading evenly across an entire system diagram?
choices: They don't — threats are equally likely anywhere in a system
Because a trust boundary is exactly where the system has to accept input or action from something it doesn't yet fully trust, which is where an attacker's influence can first enter
Because trust boundaries are always drawn incorrectly by engineers
Because trust boundaries only exist in diagrams, not in real systems
items.explanation: Inside a single trusted zone, a system is reasoning about data it already validated or generated itself. At a trust boundary, it's accepting something new from outside that zone — which is exactly the moment an attacker gets their first opportunity to influence what the system does next.
items.reference:
Untrusted: student's browser
App trust: upload API, scan queue
Storage trust: private bucket

Why: threats cluster where trust level changes, not inside a single trusted zone.

items.prompt: In Meridian's upload diagram, is the edge from the scan queue back to the storage bucket (promoting a file out of quarantine) a trust boundary crossing?
choices: Yes — it's a change in what the file is treated as (unscanned vs. cleared), even though both sides are inside the app's own infrastructure, so it's worth a deliberate check
No — trust boundaries can only exist between an external user and the system, never between two internal components
No — anything happening entirely inside 'the app trust zone' can never need a mitigation
Yes, but only if the storage bucket is hosted by a different cloud provider than the queue
items.explanation: Trust boundaries aren't only about external-vs-internal — they mark any meaningful change in what something is treated as. A file moving from 'unscanned, quarantined' to 'cleared and servable' is exactly that kind of change, which is why Meridian's threat table has a dedicated row for a file being served before its scan completes, even though both sides of that edge are internal infrastructure.
items.reference:
Untrusted: student's browser
App trust: upload API, scan queue
Storage trust: private bucket

Why: threats cluster where trust level changes, not inside a single trusted zone.

items.prompt: What does 'secure by default' mean as a design principle?
choices: Every feature must be reviewed by the security team before launch
The behavior that happens when no one configures anything should already be the safe, restrictive one — not one that requires someone to remember to lock it down later
All data must be encrypted, with no exceptions
Security features should be enabled only after a customer requests them
items.explanation: Secure by default is about what happens in the absence of explicit configuration — the unconfigured, 'nobody thought about it' state should be the safe one, since that state is common in any real codebase, not a rare edge case.
items.reference:
Permissive default

Accepts any file type unless someone later adds a blocklist

Restrictive default

Accepts nothing until an explicit allowlist is added

Why: 'nobody configured it' is the common case, not the rare one.

items.prompt: A new IAM role starts with broad read access to every table, and engineers are expected to narrow it later once they know exactly what's needed. Is this secure by default?
choices: Yes — starting broad and narrowing later is the standard secure-by-default pattern
No — this is permissive by default. Secure by default would start the role with zero access and add specific grants one at a time as they're actually needed
It depends only on how well-documented the narrowing process is
Secure by default doesn't apply to IAM roles, only to file uploads
items.explanation: Starting broad and narrowing later is exactly the permissive-by-default failure mode — it relies on someone remembering to do the narrowing step, and 'later' has a way of never quite arriving under normal workload pressure. The secure-by-default version reverses the order: start at zero, add only what's demonstrably needed.
items.reference:
Permissive default

Accepts any file type unless someone later adds a blocklist

Restrictive default

Accepts nothing until an explicit allowlist is added

Why: 'nobody configured it' is the common case, not the rare one.

items.prompt: According to this unit, where should a feature's threat model actually end up living?
choices: In a separate security team's private tracker that engineers never see
As a 'Security considerations' section inside the design doc itself, reviewed at the same gate as the scalability and cost sections
Nowhere in particular — it's a one-time discussion, not a written artifact
Only in the pull request description of the first commit
items.explanation: Writing threats into the design doc, checked at the same review gate as other design concerns, is what makes the practice durable and enforceable — a verbal discussion that never gets written down is easy to skip next time and impossible for a later engineer to find.
items.reference:
Draft + DFD→Threat-model pass→Security section written→Design review gate→Build

Why: a habit that isn't written into the process gets skipped under deadline pressure.

items.prompt: Why did Meridian's practice hold up under deadline pressure while Halcyon's presumably would not have, even if both teams cared equally about security in the abstract?
choices: Meridian's engineers were simply more senior
Meridian's design-doc template required the security section before a reviewer could approve it — the same enforcement mechanism that made the rollout plan section non-optional
Halcyon's engineers were told not to worry about security
There's no real reason — it was random which team happened to do it
items.explanation: The difference isn't individual diligence, which is unreliable under pressure for any team — it's whether the process itself makes the step a gate rather than a suggestion. A required section a reviewer checks for is far more durable than a good intention nobody enforces.
items.reference:
Draft + DFD→Threat-model pass→Security section written→Design review gate→Build

Why: a habit that isn't written into the process gets skipped under deadline pressure.

items.prompt: Who reviews the security-considerations section of a design doc, according to this unit's process?
choices: No one — it's self-certified by the author with no external check
The same design-review gate that checks scalability and cost — the process `adr-governance` and `architecture-review` already describe for architectural decisions generally
Only an external auditor hired once a year
Whoever happens to be free that week, with no consistent process
items.explanation: This unit doesn't invent a separate review process for security — it plugs the security-considerations section into the same design-review gate that already exists for other design concerns, the way `adr-governance`/`architecture-review` describe. Reusing an existing gate is what makes this durable rather than yet another standalone process to maintain.
items.reference:
Draft + DFD→Threat-model pass→Security section written→Design review gate→Build

Why: a habit that isn't written into the process gets skipped under deadline pressure.

items.prompt: A threat is described as: 'a leaked signed URL for a student's file keeps working indefinitely, letting anyone with the link view it long after it should have expired.' Which STRIDE category is this?
choices: Denial of service
Information disclosure
Repudiation
Spoofing
items.explanation: This is about data becoming visible to someone who shouldn't see it — a leaked URL exposing content beyond its intended access window is squarely Information disclosure, not a service-availability issue (DoS) or an identity-impersonation issue (Spoofing).
items.reference:
SpoofingTamperingRepudiationInfo disclosureDenial of serviceElevation of privilege

Why: mapping a real threat to its category is what makes STRIDE a checklist, not just six abstract words.

items.prompt: A threat is described as: 'a malicious file is found in production, but there's no log tying it to the account that uploaded it, so no one can determine how it got there.' Which STRIDE category is this?
choices: Repudiation
Tampering
Elevation of privilege
Denial of service
items.explanation: Repudiation is specifically about the inability to prove who did what — the absence of an audit trail linking the upload to an account is exactly that gap, distinct from Tampering (data being modified unexpectedly) or the file itself gaining excess privilege.
items.reference:
SpoofingTamperingRepudiationInfo disclosureDenial of serviceElevation of privilege

Why: mapping a real threat to its category is what makes STRIDE a checklist, not just six abstract words.

items.prompt: A threat is described as: 'a single account uploads tens of thousands of large files in a loop, exhausting storage space and backing up the scan queue for every other student.' Which STRIDE category is this?
choices: Information disclosure
Spoofing
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege
items.explanation: This is about making the system unusable for legitimate users through resource exhaustion — the definition of Denial of service, regardless of whether the account doing it is legitimate or compromised.
items.reference:
SpoofingTamperingRepudiationInfo disclosureDenial of serviceElevation of privilege

Why: mapping a real threat to its category is what makes STRIDE a checklist, not just six abstract words.

items.prompt: In Meridian's data-flow diagram, why is the edge from the student's browser to the upload API called the single riskiest edge in the whole diagram?
choices: Because it uses the slowest network connection
Because it's the only edge where the system accepts something from a party it doesn't yet fully trust — every other edge is between components already inside the app's own trust zones
Because uploads are always larger than downloads
Because that edge is drawn in red in the diagram
items.explanation: Every other edge in the diagram connects components that already trust each other to some degree (the API and the storage bucket, the scan queue and the bucket). The student's browser is the one party the system hasn't validated yet, which is exactly what makes that first crossing the highest-risk point structurally, not just by convention.
items.reference:
Untrusted: student's browser
App trust: upload API, scan queue
Storage trust: private bucket
Internal trust: signed-URL CDN, instructor

Why: the edge with the least established trust carries the most threat weight.

items.prompt: Does the edge from the instructor's browser requesting a signed URL cross a trust boundary, given the instructor is already an authenticated user of the system?
choices: No — once someone is authenticated anywhere in the system, no further edge involving them can be a trust boundary

Yes — being authenticated generally doesn't mean authorized for this specific course's files, so the request still crosses into a zone that must check whether this instructor should see this file before issuing a link
No — trust boundaries only apply to anonymous users, never to logged-in ones
Yes, but only because instructors use a different login page than students
items.explanation: Authentication (who is this) and authorization (should this specific request be allowed) are different questions, and a trust boundary can still exist between them — an authenticated instructor from a different course requesting a signed URL is exactly the Spoofing-adjacent threat Meridian's table names, which is why an authorization check runs before any link is issued.
items.reference:
Untrusted: student's browser
App trust: upload API, scan queue
Storage trust: private bucket
Internal trust: signed-URL CDN, instructor

Why: the edge with the least established trust carries the most threat weight.

items.prompt: A teammate suggests skipping the DFD step entirely and just discussing threats from memory, since the team already knows the system. What's lost by skipping the diagram?
choices: Nothing — the diagram is purely decorative and adds no real value
A shared, explicit picture of every edge and trust boundary, which is what keeps the STRIDE walkthrough systematic instead of only covering whichever parts of the system happen to come to mind first
The diagram is required by law for any system handling personal data
Diagrams are only useful for onboarding new engineers, not for threat modeling
items.explanation: Threat modeling from memory tends to cover the parts of a system that are top of mind and miss the rest — exactly the failure mode a DFD prevents by forcing every edge to be drawn and therefore considered. The diagram isn't decoration; it's the checklist's actual scope, which is why L2 draws it before asking a single STRIDE question.
items.reference:
Untrusted: student's browser
App trust: upload API, scan queue
Storage trust: private bucket
Internal trust: signed-URL CDN, instructor

Why: the edge with the least established trust carries the most threat weight.

items.prompt: Which mitigation directly addresses a Tampering threat where an attacker forges a file's content-type header to disguise a script as a PDF?
choices: Rate-limiting the upload endpoint
Sniffing the file's actual content server-side (magic bytes) instead of trusting the client-supplied header or extension
Issuing short-lived signed URLs for downloads
Logging every upload with the account id and timestamp
items.explanation: The threat is specifically about a client-controlled claim (the header) not matching reality. Content sniffing verifies the actual bytes independent of what the client claims, which is what closes this exact gap — rate limiting and signed URLs address different threats entirely (DoS and information disclosure, respectively).
items.reference:
Tampering (forged type) → content sniffing. DoS (flood) → size cap + rate limit. Info disclosure (guessable key) → random UUID keys. Repudiation (no record) → audit log

Why: each mitigation is chosen because it closes a specific named threat, not as a generic best practice.

items.prompt: Which mitigation directly addresses an Information disclosure threat where one student could guess another student's file location?
choices: A per-account rate limit on uploads
Random, non-sequential storage keys instead of filename-derived or sequential ones
A magic-byte content check on the uploaded file
An audit log recording who uploaded each file
items.explanation: Guessability is the core of this threat — a predictable key (like the original filename or a sequential id) can be enumerated or guessed. Random, unpredictable keys remove that avenue directly; the other listed mitigations address different threats (DoS, tampering, and repudiation respectively).
items.reference:
Tampering (forged type) → content sniffing. DoS (flood) → size cap + rate limit. Info disclosure (guessable key) → random UUID keys. Repudiation (no record) → audit log

Why: each mitigation is chosen because it closes a specific named threat, not as a generic best practice.

items.prompt: A teammate argues secure-by-default just moves configuration effort from 'restrict it later' to 'grant it now,' so total work is unchanged — does that mean secure-by-default provides no real benefit?
choices: Yes — if total configuration effort is unchanged, there's no meaningful benefit

No — the benefit isn't about total effort, it's about which direction a *forgotten* step fails in: permissive-by-default fails open (a real gap), restrictive-by-default fails closed (an inconvenience, not a breach)
Yes, but only for file uploads specifically, not for IAM roles
No, because restrictive-by-default always requires strictly less total configuration than permissive-by-default
items.explanation: The real claim isn't about total effort — it's about the failure mode when a step gets skipped, which happens routinely in any real codebase. A skipped 'restrict later' step under permissive defaults leaves something open to anyone; a skipped 'grant now' step under restrictive defaults just leaves something unusable until someone notices, a far cheaper mistake.
items.reference:
Permissive, forgotten step

Fails open — stays broadly accessible

Restrictive, forgotten step

Fails closed — stays unusable until fixed

Why: the direction a mistake fails in matters more than whether a mistake happens at all.

items.prompt: Why does this unit say a permissive-by-default field is especially risky in a large, real codebase specifically, more than in a small toy example?
choices: Because larger codebases always have worse engineers

Because 'someone forgot to configure it' becomes statistically likely as the number of fields, roles, and endpoints grows — a permissive default multiplies that likelihood across every one of them, while a restrictive default caps the damage of any single miss
Because permissive defaults only exist in large codebases, never in small ones
Large codebases are actually less risky because they have more reviewers
items.explanation: The risk of a permissive default doesn't stay constant as a system grows — it compounds, because every new field, role, or endpoint is another chance for someone to skip the 'now go lock it down' step under real deadline pressure. Restrictive defaults don't eliminate mistakes, but they cap what a single missed step actually exposes.
items.reference:
Permissive, forgotten step

Fails open — stays broadly accessible

Restrictive, forgotten step

Fails closed — stays unusable until fixed

Why: the direction a mistake fails in matters more than whether a mistake happens at all.

items.prompt: This unit argues threat modeling should be time-boxed (Meridian's took 30 minutes) rather than open-ended. Why does the time-box matter for whether the practice survives long-term?
choices: Because longer threat models are always less accurate
Because a practice that can't fit inside a normal sprint will get skipped under real deadline pressure, which defeats the point of having it as a standard step at all
Because regulations mandate a maximum of 30 minutes for any security review
Time-boxing doesn't actually matter, only thoroughness does
items.explanation: A process only survives contact with a real deadline if it's cheap enough to not feel like a workstream of its own. An open-ended threat model invites 'we don't have time for that this sprint' — a 30-minute, time-boxed pass is small enough to become a habit rather than a special request.
items.reference:
Time-box itState the alternative costScope the ask

Why: making the trade-off legible is what keeps the practice from being skipped under pressure.

items.prompt: A product manager asks why every design, including a small copy tweak, needs a full STRIDE pass. What's the right response, per this unit's guidance on scoping the ask?
choices: Yes, every change of any size needs a full STRIDE pass, no exceptions

No — reserve the full pass for designs that introduce a new trust boundary, data flow, or user-controlled input; a copy tweak that crosses none of those doesn't need one, which keeps the practice proportionate
Threat modeling should never apply to anything the product team is involved in
The PM should be told to stop asking and simply accept whatever the security team decides
items.explanation: Applying a full threat-modeling pass to every change regardless of risk turns a proportionate practice into a blanket tax, which erodes goodwill and eventually gets the whole practice pushed back on. Scoping it to changes that actually introduce new trust boundaries or data flows keeps the ask matched to the actual risk.
items.reference:
Time-box itState the alternative costScope the ask

Why: making the trade-off legible is what keeps the practice from being skipped under pressure.

items.prompt: Why is 'state the alternative cost, not just the up-front cost' a more persuasive argument to a non-security stakeholder than simply asserting 'security is important'?
choices: Because it isn't more persuasive — assertions of importance work just as well

Because it translates the trade-off into terms the stakeholder already reasons in — comparing 30 minutes now against an emergency fix, a pentest finding, and a customer conversation later, rather than an abstract value claim they have no way to weigh
Because stakeholders are legally required to accept cost-based arguments
Because it removes the need for any actual mitigation work
items.explanation: A bare assertion ('security matters') gives a PM nothing to weigh against a ship date. Naming the realistic later cost — using this unit's own Meridian/Halcyon numbers — puts the trade-off in the same currency (time, cost, customer trust) the stakeholder already uses to make other calls, which is the actual translation `translating-technical-risk-business-risk` teaches generally.
items.reference:
Time-box itState the alternative costScope the ask

Why: making the trade-off legible is what keeps the practice from being skipped under pressure.

items.prompt: Meridian's full threat table covers Tampering, DoS, Information disclosure, Elevation of privilege, Spoofing, and Repudiation across its 8 rows. A reviewer notices no row explicitly discusses whether an instructor can be fooled into approving a fraudulent enrollment request tied to the upload flow. Is this a real gap in the table, or already covered?
choices: It's already covered under the Spoofing row about signed-URL requests, no further action needed

It's a real, distinct threat the current table doesn't cover — enrollment approval is a separate flow the DFD didn't include, so it was never walked through STRIDE at all, and the fix is to extend the DFD, not to stretch an existing row to cover it
It's out of scope by definition, since STRIDE only ever applies to file-upload features
It's not a real threat because instructors are always trusted by definition
items.explanation: This is exactly the kind of gap threat modeling exists to catch: if the DFD never included the enrollment-approval flow, STRIDE was never asked against it, and no row in the table addresses it. The fix isn't to retroactively stretch the Spoofing row (which is about a different flow, requesting signed URLs) — it's to extend the diagram to include the missing flow and threat-model it on its own terms.
items.reference:
8-row table covers upload, storage, scan, and signed-URL flows only — a flow not drawn in the DFD was never asked the six STRIDE questions at all

Why: a threat table is only as complete as the diagram it was built from.

items.prompt: The threat table lists a mitigation for 'a file is served before the malware scan completes' (quarantine-then-promote), but doesn't have a row for 'the malware scan itself is unavailable or backlogged for hours.' Is this second scenario the same threat, already covered, or a distinct gap?
choices: The same threat — quarantine-then-promote already handles any scenario involving the scan step

A distinct gap — the existing row assumes the scan eventually completes and just shouldn't be bypassed early; it says nothing about what happens to legitimate uploads if the scan queue itself is unavailable or severely delayed, which is closer to a Denial of service question
Not a real concern, since scan queues never go down in practice
Already fully covered under the Information disclosure row about signed URLs
items.explanation: Quarantine-then-promote answers 'don't serve it early' — it says nothing about what a legitimate student experiences if the scan backs up for hours (files stuck in limbo, effectively unusable). That's a distinct question, closer to Denial of service against legitimate use than to the Tampering concern the existing row addresses, and would need its own row and mitigation (e.g. a queue depth alert and a fallback SLA).
items.reference:
8-row table covers upload, storage, scan, and signed-URL flows only — a flow not drawn in the DFD was never asked the six STRIDE questions at all

Why: a threat table is only as complete as the diagram it was built from.

items.prompt: A teammate proposes closing every possible gap by adding rows for every STRIDE category against every element, even ones where no plausible threat exists, 'just to be thorough.' Is this the right way to make the table more complete?
choices: Yes — a table is only complete once every category has been applied to every element with a written row, regardless of plausibility

No — the goal is asking all six questions to make sure nothing plausible is missed, not padding the table with rows for implausible combinations; a table cluttered with non-threats makes the real rows harder to find and review
Yes, because reviewers are specifically trained to skip irrelevant rows quickly
No, because STRIDE should only ever be applied to exactly one element per system
items.explanation: Asking all six questions at each element is a discipline for not missing something real — it's not a mandate to record a row for every category regardless of plausibility. A table padded with implausible entries is harder for a reviewer to actually use, which works against the same goal (a table that gets genuinely read and enforced) that motivated writing it into the design doc in the first place.
items.reference:
8-row table covers upload, storage, scan, and signed-URL flows only — a flow not drawn in the DFD was never asked the six STRIDE questions at all

Why: a threat table is only as complete as the diagram it was built from.

items.prompt: Meridian rated 'uploaded file executes with the app's own service-account privileges' as Low likelihood / Critical impact, while 'unbounded upload size exhausts storage' was rated Medium likelihood / Medium impact. Why might a team still prioritize mitigating the first one despite its lower likelihood?
choices: Likelihood should always outweigh impact when prioritizing, so the second threat should be fixed first

A Critical-impact threat, even at low likelihood, can represent a much larger expected cost than a Medium/Medium one, and some Critical-impact outcomes (full privilege escalation) are severe enough that a team may choose to mitigate them regardless of exact probability
Impact ratings are purely subjective and shouldn't influence prioritization at all
Low-likelihood threats should never be mitigated, only tracked
items.explanation: Severity is a function of both likelihood and impact together, not likelihood alone — a rare but catastrophic outcome (full elevation of privilege) can justify mitigation ahead of a more common but bounded one, especially when the mitigation itself (denying execute permission on the bucket) is cheap relative to the risk it removes.
items.reference:
Low/Critical (execute privilege) vs. Medium/Medium (storage exhaustion) — likelihood and impact are both inputs, not a single ranking by one alone

Why: prioritization weighs both axes, and a cheap mitigation can justify acting on a low-likelihood/high-impact row first.

items.prompt: Two threats both get rated Medium/High. One's mitigation takes an afternoon; the other's mitigation requires a multi-week infrastructure change. Does an identical severity rating mean both should be tackled with equal urgency?
choices: Yes — identical severity ratings always imply identical urgency regardless of mitigation cost

Not necessarily — severity says how much the threat matters, but sequencing which gets fixed first can reasonably also weigh how cheaply and quickly each can actually be closed, especially when the cheap one can be shipped immediately at near-zero opportunity cost
No — the harder-to-fix threat should always be deprioritized indefinitely in favor of the easy one
Severity ratings are meaningless once mitigation cost is considered at all
items.explanation: Severity tells a team how much a threat matters if left unaddressed; it doesn't by itself dictate sequencing. It's a reasonable, defensible call to ship the cheap Medium/High mitigation immediately while scoping the expensive one properly — as long as that sequencing decision is made deliberately and visibly, not used as a permanent excuse to never get to the harder fix.
items.reference:
Low/Critical (execute privilege) vs. Medium/Medium (storage exhaustion) — likelihood and impact are both inputs, not a single ranking by one alone

Why: prioritization weighs both axes, and a cheap mitigation can justify acting on a low-likelihood/high-impact row first.

items.prompt: Implement `isAllowedExtension(filename, allowedExtensions)`: given a filename string and an array of allowed extensions (e.g. `['.pdf', '.docx']`, always lowercase, always including the leading dot), return `true` only if the filename's extension (case-insensitively) is in the allowlist. This is a deny-by-default check — an empty or missing extension must return `false`, never `true`.

tests.description: allows a matching extension
denies an extension not in the allowlist
matches case-insensitively
denies a filename with no extension at all

items.explanation: The deny-by-default shape matters as much as the matching logic: the function only ever returns `true` when the extension is explicitly found in the allowlist — there's no fallback branch that defaults to permitting an unrecognized or missing extension. A file with no dot, or a dot as the very last character, is treated as having no valid extension and denied, rather than silently matching some default case.
items.reference:
const ALLOWED = new Set(['.pdf', '.docx', '.txt']); if (!ALLOWED.has(extension)) return res.status(400)...

Why: deny-by-default means the safe answer is the one that requires no configuration to reach.

items.prompt: Implement `buildStorageKey(originalName, generateId)`: given the client-supplied original filename and a zero-argument function `generateId` that returns a fresh random id string, return a storage key that (a) never includes any part of `originalName` itself, and (b) preserves the original file's extension (lowercased), in the form `<generated-id><extension>`. If `originalName` has no extension, return just `<generated-id>` with no trailing dot.

tests.description: uses the generated id, not the original name, and preserves a lowercased extension
never leaks any substring of the original filename into the key
handles a filename with no extension by omitting the trailing dot

items.explanation: The only piece of `originalName` that survives into the storage key is its extension — never the stem, never any casing or wording from the original title. This is exactly what closes Meridian's Information disclosure row: a key built this way can't be guessed from knowing (or even seeing) the original filename, unlike Halcyon's version, which stored the file under that filename directly.

flags even when the id appears as a small substring elsewhere

items.prompt: Implement `isSignedUrlValid(issuedAtMs, nowMs, ttlMs)`: return `true` only if the current time (`nowMs`) is strictly before `issuedAtMs + ttlMs` — that is, the URL hasn't yet expired. A `nowMs` exactly equal to or after the expiry moment must return `false`.

tests.description: valid well before expiry
invalid exactly at the expiry moment
invalid after expiry

items.explanation: Using a strict less-than at the exact expiry boundary matters: a URL that's valid 'through' its expiry moment (using <=) technically extends its usable window by one instant, and more importantly signals a boundary condition that's easy to get backwards under pressure. Strict less-than means the moment the TTL is reached, the URL is already invalid — matching Meridian's 10-minute signed URLs closing the leaked-link Information disclosure row from L3's threat table.
items.reference:
Signed URLs expire in 10 minutes, scoped to one object — closes the 'leaked link keeps working indefinitely' row

Why: an expiry check that's off by one boundary condition quietly widens the window it was meant to close.

items.prompt: Implement `remainingTtlMs(issuedAtMs, nowMs, ttlMs)`: return how many milliseconds remain before the signed URL expires. If the URL has already expired, return `0` rather than a negative number.

tests.description: returns remaining time before expiry
returns 0 exactly at expiry
returns 0, not negative, after expiry

items.explanation: Flooring at zero rather than returning a negative number matters for whatever calls this function downstream — a raw negative 'remaining time' invites a caller to mistakenly treat it as truthy or to display a nonsensical negative countdown, when the correct behavior is simply 'no time remains, treat as expired,' which `Math.max(0, ...)` enforces at the source instead of relying on every caller to remember the check.

items.prompt: Implement `hasPermission(grantedPermissions, requiredPermission)`: given an array of permission strings a role has been explicitly granted, and a single required permission string, return `true` only if `requiredPermission` appears in `grantedPermissions`. An empty or missing `grantedPermissions` array must return `false` for any required permission — never treat 'no grants recorded' as 'everything allowed.'

tests.description: allows an explicitly granted permission
denies a permission not in the granted list
denies everything when grantedPermissions is empty

items.explanation: The `Array.isArray` guard means a missing or malformed `grantedPermissions` value (undefined, null, a typo'd object) fails closed rather than throwing or, worse, being coerced into something that accidentally grants access. This is the same restrictive-by-default shape as the file-upload allowlist — the function has exactly one path to `true` (an explicit match) and every other path denies.

A new role starts with zero permissions and gains them one named grant at a time — never broad-by-default waiting to be narrowed

Why: a permission check with only one path to 'allow' is far easier to reason about than one with multiple.

Neither input array may be mutated. If `additionalGrants` is omitted, return a copy of `baseRole` unchanged.

does not mutate the original baseRole array
tests.expr: expect((() => { const base = ['read:files']; mergeRolePermissions(base, ['write:files']); return base; })()).toEqual(['read:files'])

items.explanation: This function only ever grows a role's permission set by explicit union — there's no path where a call to it silently removes an existing restriction or defaults to a broader set than what was passed in. Not mutating either input matters in a real codebase for the same reason as the rest of this unit: a shared array that gets silently mutated by one caller is exactly the kind of implicit, easy-to-miss side effect that erodes confidence in what a permission set actually contains.

items.prompt: Implement `requiresExplicitPublicFlag(config)`: given a config object that may have a `public` boolean field, return `true` (meaning: this endpoint is public, auth is skipped) only if `config.public === true` exactly. Any other value — `undefined`, `'true'` the string, `1`, missing field entirely — must return `false`, meaning auth is required.

tests.description: public true (boolean) skips auth
missing field requires auth
truthy but non-boolean value still requires auth

items.explanation: Using strict equality against the literal boolean `true` (rather than a truthy check) closes off an entire class of accidental-exposure bugs where a config value like the string `'true'`, the number `1`, or an unrelated truthy object would otherwise slip through and skip authentication. The unusual case — public access — is the one that has to be spelled out exactly right; everything else, including any ambiguity, defaults to requiring auth.
